Wilt
wilt
v. (second person singular of will; rendering Hebrew imperfect of volition, Greek theleis and the future)
From Saxon wilt, second person singular of willan, to will or desire. Its root sense is volition, as the root sense of shall is obligation — a distinction the older grammarians guarded carefully and modern usage has lost. Distinguish it from the unrelated verb to wilt, to droop.

Biblical Definition

Wilt is the second person singular of will, and its proper force is desire or determination rather than bare futurity. Abram uses it to press God about the promise: “Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless” (Genesis 15:2), and the answer is the covenant of the seed and the stars. The psalmists use it to hold God to His own character: “With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright” (2 Samuel 22:26); “For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous” (Psalm 5:12). They also use it to complain of delay without abandoning faith: “O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people?” (Psalm 80:4). In the Gospels the word most often falls from Christ's lips as a question that requires the hearer to state what he actually wants — the servants asking whether they shall gather the tares, the blind man asked what he would have done, the impotent man at the pool asked whether he wills to be made whole. Scripture takes the human will seriously enough to interrogate it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second person singular of will; used only with thou. Its root sense is volition and determination, as distinguished from the obligation carried by shalt. In Scripture it frames Abram's question about the promise, the psalmist's appeal to God's character, and Christ's questions to those who came to Him.

WILT, v. [Sax. wilt.] The second person singular of will; as, thou wilt.

2. The primary sense of will is to desire, to be inclined, to determine; hence its use in promise and resolution.

3. In the first person it expresses determination; in the second and third, prediction or permission.

4. WILT, v.i. To begin to wither; to lose freshness. This is a wholly distinct word.

5. In Scripture, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless? Gen. 15; how long wilt thou be angry? Psa. 80.

Key Scripture

Genesis 15:2 — "And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?"

2 Samuel 22:26 — "With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, and with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright."

Psalm 80:4 — "O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people?"

Psalm 5:12 — "For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield."

Modern Corruption

The will of man is the point where two errors meet: a libertarian free will that makes the sinner the deciding cause of his own salvation, and a fatalism that treats his willing as unreal. Scripture's questions — wilt thou be made whole? — presuppose a will that genuinely chooses and is genuinely bound.

expand to see more

The Reformed doctrine is not that man has no will but that his will is not free toward God until it is freed. The 1689 Confession states it exactly: man by his fall into a state of sin has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation, and is not able by his own strength to convert himself; when God converts a sinner He frees him from his natural bondage and enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. The sinner therefore always does what he wills, and what he wills is sin, until grace renews the willing itself. Arminian theology grants the fallen will a decisive vote it does not possess; the result is a salvation that finally depends on the creature.

The pastoral consequence is not passivity but the opposite. Because the will is real, Christ questions it: Wilt thou be made whole? He asks a man who had lain thirty-eight years by the pool. Because the will is bound, the answer must be given by grace. Preachers therefore command what only God can grant, and they are right to do so, since the command is the very instrument the Spirit uses. Whosoever will may come; and that any man wills to come is itself the evidence of a work already begun in him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew expresses volition by the imperfect, sometimes strengthened by 'abah (to be willing) or chaphets (to delight in); Greek uses thelo and boulomai for willing and the future indicative for simple futurity.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'abah (H14) — to be willing, to consent; almost always used in the negative of Israel's refusal.

Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight in, to take pleasure in; the willing that arises from desire rather than duty.

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to wish, to desire; the verb in Christ's questions to those who sought Him.

Greek boulomai (G1014) — to purpose, to determine; willing considered as settled counsel.

Saxon willan — to will or desire; the root that distinguishes will from shall, which means to owe.

Usage

"Of pressing God about an unfulfilled promise: what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless? (Genesis 15:2)."

"Of appealing to God's consistency with His own character: With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful (2 Samuel 22:26)."

"Of complaint at delay that does not abandon faith: how long wilt thou be angry against the prayer of thy people? (Psalm 80:4)."
